provenance: Opus 5.5 subscription CLI draft with host review/repairs, source restrictions and execution verification.

draft_notes.explanation: Original rule: colour 1 is the anchor and stays put. Every other non-background colour, taken as one whole shape (all of its cells), slides along the row axis until its leading edge (min row) lines up with the anchor's min row. Columns are kept, and each shape is erased and redrawn. In visible coordinates the factory hard-codes the colour roles as background = palette[0], anchor = palette[1] and movers = palette[2] and palette[4]. Any other non-background colour that appears is also moved, matching the archived solver. The factory also picks the axis and edge from d4. The reflection reverses columns before rotating, so it never changes the original row axis; only the rotation count matters. With k = 0 the shapes move along rows and align their minimum row. With k = 1 they move along columns and align the maximum column. With k = 2 they move along rows and align the maximum row. With k = 3 they move along columns and align the minimum column. The three shapes in this generator are identical copies, so aligning either edge gives the same result. The emitted program uses the edge that the original 'top' maps to. Cells pushed outside the grid are clipped, as in the archived solver. That never happens in the generator's domain, because every shape fits inside the grid and the anchor's span is a valid position.
draft_notes.limitations: The program assumes each non-anchor colour forms a single shape, as the generator guarantees; all cells of a colour move together even when they are only diagonally connected. If the anchor colour is missing, the input is returned unchanged. It relies on shapes occupying disjoint ranges perpendicular to the motion axis, which the generator ensures, so erasing and redrawing never overwrites another shape. The fixtures are consistent with the uniform rule. No tests were run.
